info.title: What is &kdump; and how does it use &kexec;?

abstract.para: &kdump; does not save the dump from the crashed kernel itself. It starts a second kernel with &kexec; and saves the dump from there.

section.title: How &kdump; uses &kexec;
section.para: &kexec; is the mechanism: a system call and the kexec command, which load a kernel into memory and start it directly, without going through the firmware (BIOS/UEFI) and the boot loader. &kdump; is the service built around this mechanism. It adds everything else that is needed to capture a crash:

listitem.para: A reserved area of memory for a second kernel, the capture kernel.
An initramfs for the capture kernel that contains the tools to save the dump.
The configuration that defines how the dump is saved, locally or on a remote target.

section.para: When the system boots and later crashes, the following happens:

listitem.para: At boot, the kernel reserves an area of memory for the capture kernel. The size comes from the crashkernel= option on the kernel command line.
kdump.service loads the capture kernel and its initramfs into the reserved area with kexec -p. The capture kernel stays idle.
When the running kernel panics, it uses &kexec; to start the capture kernel. The firmware and the boot loader do not run, so the memory of the crashed kernel stays intact.
The capture kernel saves that memory to a vmcore file, together with the kernel log, and reboots the system.

section.para: Enabling &kdump; does not change normal reboots. &kdump; loads the capture kernel only for a crash, so a normal reboot still goes through the firmware and the boot loader. You can also use &kexec; on its own to reboot faster, as described in the separate article Using Kexec for Faster Reboots.

section.title: The dual-kernel model
section.para: &kdump; relies on two kernels being involved in a crash:

listitem.para: The production kernel is the kernel that normally runs your system and its workloads.

The capture kernel (also called the crash kernel or &kdump; kernel) is a second, minimal kernel image with its own initramfs. &kdump; builds the initramfs so that it contains the drivers and tools, such as makedumpfile, needed to save the dump.

section.para: When the production kernel panics, it can no longer be trusted to write its own crash information to disk: its data structures may be corrupted, and a normal reboot would overwrite the memory you are trying to inspect. Because the capture kernel runs from its own reserved memory region, the production kernel's memory contents remain intact and readable while the capture kernel is running.

section.title: What does a captured vmcore file contain?
section.para: Once the capture kernel is running, it writes the production kernel's memory contents to a file called vmcore, together with a copy of the kernel's ring buffer log (dmesg) from the moment of the crash. Depending on the dump level set with KDUMP_DUMPLEVEL (see ), a vmcore file can contain:

listitem.para: Kernel state: active kernel data structures, global variables and the call stack that was executing at the moment of the crash.
Process information: the list of processes that were running, along with their individual stacks and registers.
Memory pages: the actual data held in RAM by the kernel and by user-space applications.

VMCOREINFO: a section that records how the kernel's memory was laid out, such as the kernel release, the page size and the addresses of kernel symbols, so that analysis tools can interpret the raw memory.

section.para: You analyze this file after the system has rebooted, using tools such as crash or GDB. See for details.
